absent: Numeric values of small-map and large-map extent limits, page size, identifier width, and flag bit positions.
Semantics of parent-map range translation, file versus task capability checks, and identity conversion helpers.
Full layouts of task, credential, file, seq_file, namespace proxy, common namespace, and ucounts structures.
Sysctl string processing, poll notification mechanics, entropy mixing guarantees, and registration lifetime.
Slab cache parameters, allocation flags, sorting implementation, and deferred reclaim timing.
Initial allow state establishment for groups control and owner field initialization for new namespaces.
Error pointer encoding and propagation rules for namespace lookup failures.

findings.text: Identifier maps are exposed through sequential iteration interfaces, one per identifier class. Each interface supplies start, advance, display and teardown roles. Start selects the map of the namespace attached to the stream. Display renders one extent as upper start with translated lower start and length. Advance moves the file position forward and restarts. Teardown does nothing.

An identifier map keeps a published count plus two storage forms. Small populations use embedded slots. Larger populations use separately allocated forward and reverse arrays. An extent carries an upper start, a lower start and a length. The count is the publication signal for lock-free readers.

Sequential tables bind a position-based start role, a teardown role, an advance role and a per-item display role. Control tables bind a textual name, a data pointer, a length limit, a permission mode, a handler and an optional poll object.

Iteration start enforces ordering before reading the count, then reports end of stream for positions at or beyond that count. In-range positions resolve to embedded storage while the total stays within the small-map threshold, otherwise to the matching slot of the extended forward array.

Extent display resolves the viewing namespace from the stream, substituting its parent when viewer equals target and a parent exists. The stored lower value is converted from kernel representation to viewer-relative form before emission with upper start and length.

A candidate extent is rejected when its upper interval intersects any accepted upper interval or its lower interval intersects any accepted lower interval. Bounds are inclusive from start through start plus length minus one, and every accepted extent is checked regardless of storage form.

Appending preserves existing entries. At inline capacity a large forward array is allocated and inline contents copied into it while reverse storage stays absent. The new extent is stored at the index given by the count and the count grows by one. Allocation failure leaves the map unchanged.

Small maps need no ordering. Large maps keep forward storage ordered by upper start and a duplicated array ordered by lower start for reverse search. The duplicate covers only the populated prefix. Each ordering compares only its respective start field with a three-way result.

Writes to the three map files share a common writer but differ in privilege class. The initial namespace rejects all writes. A viewer that is neither target nor its parent is rejected. User and group classes use privileged handling while the project class is explicitly unprivileged.

The common writer accepts only one write at offset zero with length below one page. Input is split into lines each expecting three decimal numbers with whitespace separation and no trailing material. Sentinel maximum starts, zero or wrapping lengths, overlapping ranges, exceeding the global extent limit, and empty results all cause rejection.

After parsing the candidate undergoes permission validation and translation of each lower start through the parent map, where unmappable ranges fail. Large candidates are ordered for lookup. Installation copies inline data or transfers ownership of extended arrays, issues a write barrier, then publishes the count and reports the input length. Only a previously empty map may be installed.

An extra privilege check applies only when some extent maps lower zero. Writing to an unshared own namespace then requires a recorded parent capability flag. Writing to a child namespace requires the file opener to hold filesystem capability against the parent of the target.

A single one-length extent owned by the writer may be installed when it maps the writer own identity as seen in the parent namespace. The group variant additionally requires that groups-allowed mode has not been withdrawn. Capability-less requests are otherwise accepted, while privileged requests need the capability held both by the parent of the target and by the file opener.

The groups control shows allow or deny and starts in allow. Writing deny moves permanently to deny unless a group map already exists, when it is refused. Writing allow succeeds only while still in allow and never re-enables after deny. Writes must start at zero, fit a tiny buffer, name exactly one word, and allow only trailing whitespace.

All map installations and groups-flag mutations are serialized by one global user-namespace state mutex. Extent readers and groups display do not take it. Extent readers rely on a read barrier paired with the writer write barrier plus a count-then-data dependency. Groups display uses a single atomic load.

User namespace attachment provides reference-counted retrieval and release, with retrieval under read-side protection. Installation refuses the current namespace, multi-threaded callers, shared filesystem context, missing administrative capability over the destination, and missing destination credentials. On success it transfers the namespace reference into the credential and establishes new usage accounting.

Ownership lookup returns the owning user namespace only when the caller user namespace appears on the ancestor chain from that owner upward. A missing ancestor yields permission failure. The owner of a user namespace is defined as its parent.
A membership helper reports whether the caller current user namespace is contained within a supplied target namespace.

UTS objects are reference counted. Retrieval under task protection returns a held reference or absent when no proxy exists. Release drops the reference. Installation needs administrative capability in both the destination user namespace and the credential user namespace, then swaps the proxy pointer with reference transfer. Destruction detaches from the global tree, releases usage and user references, frees common state and defers final reclaim by a grace period.

User-namespace retrieval is protected by a read-side critical section. UTS retrieval is protected by task locking around proxy access. UTS string access uses a dedicated semaphore in shared mode for sampling and exclusive mode for publication, with string conversion done outside the held lock.

Namespace type descriptors name the type and bind retrieval, release, installation and owner callbacks, with the user type also binding a parent lookup. Both caches are created at boot with accounting and panic-on-failure behaviour and the initial instances join the global tree. The UTS cache restricts copying to its name region and its pointer is read-only after init.

UTS sysctl handling resolves a per-namespace string by rebasing an initial-namespace address into the caller namespace. Access operates on a bounded temporary sampled under shared access, with string processing unlocked. On write the temporary contributes to device entropy, is copied back under exclusive access, and poll waiters are notified. One configuration disables the handler entirely.

Under the kernel directory six entries exist for arch, ostype, osrelease, version, hostname and domainname. The first four use read-only mode 0444. Hostname and domainname use mode 0644 and each links its own poll object. All dispatch through the UTS string handler.

Failed installation after extended allocation releases allocated arrays and resets destination pointers and count to empty. Readers observe either pre-installation empty or fully ordered post-installation state, never a partial count. Parallel writes at nonzero offsets to one UTS string can interleave because the lock is dropped between sampling and publication.
